messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\left\lfloor \sqrt n\right\rfloor,\qquad F=m!.
\]

We need

\[
n \mid F^{n!}+450.
\]

---

### 1. Prime powers coming from primes \(\le m\)

Suppose \(p^a\mid n\) and \(p\le m\). Then \(p\mid F\), so

\[
p^{n!}\mid F^{n!}.
\]

Also, since \(p^a\mid n\), we have \(p^a\le n\). Because \(p\ge 2\), this gives \(a\le n\le n!\). Hence

\[
p^a\mid F^{n!}.
\]

Therefore, from \(p^a\mid F^{n!}+450\), we must have

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

So the part of \(n\) made up of prime powers whose primes are \(\le m\) must divide

\[
450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2.
\]

---

### 2. Prime factors larger than \(m\)

Since

\[
m^2\le n<(m+1)^2,
\]

the integer \(n\) cannot contain two prime factors, counting multiplicity, both larger than \(m\). Thus

\[
n=R\quad\text{or}\quad n=Rq,
\]

where \(R\mid 450\), and \(q\) is either \(1\) or a prime with \(q>m\).

Now suppose \(q>m\) is a prime divisor of \(n\). Since \(q\mid n\), we have \(q-1\le n\), so \(q-1\mid n!\). Also \(q\nmid F=m!\), because \(q>m\). By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
F^{q-1}\equiv 1\pmod q.
\]

Since \(q-1\mid n!\), it follows that

\[
F^{n!}\equiv 1\pmod q.
\]

Thus

\[
F^{n!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\pmod q,
\]

so

\[
q\mid 451=11\cdot 41.
\]

Therefore any prime factor of \(n\) larger than \(m\) must be either \(11\) or \(41\).

---

### 3. Bounding \(n\)

- If there is no such prime factor, then \(n\mid 450\), so \(n\le 450\).

- If the large prime is \(q=11\), then \(m\le 10\), so

  \[
  n<(m+1)^2\le 121,
  \]

  hence \(n\le 120\).

- If the large prime is \(q=41\), then \(m\le 40\), so

  \[
  n<(m+1)^2\le 41^2=1681.
  \]

  Writing \(n=41R\) with \(R\mid 450\), we get

  \[
  R=\frac{n}{41}<41.
  \]

  The largest divisor of \(450\) strictly less than \(41\) is \(30\). Hence

  \[
  n=41R\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
  \]

So every possible \(n\) satisfies \(n\le 1230\).

---

### 4. Verifying \(n=1230\)

We have

\[
1230=30\cdot 41,
\]

and

\[
35^2=1225<1230<1296=36^2,
\]

so

\[
m=\left\lfloor \sqrt{1230}\right\rfloor=35.
\]

Check modulo \(30\):

\[
35!\text{ is divisible by }30,
\]

so

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 0\pmod{30},
\]

and

\[
450\equiv 0\pmod{30}.
\]

Thus

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 0\pmod{30}.
\]

Check modulo \(41\):

Since \(41\nmid 35!\) and \(40\mid 1230!\), Fermat gives

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1\pmod{41}.
\]

Also,

\[
451=11\cdot 41,
\]

so

\[
450\equiv -1\pmod{41}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1-1=0\pmod{41}.
\]

Since \(\gcd(30,41)=1\), we get

\[
1230\mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

Thus the largest possible value is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
